title: Poisoning / Toxin Ingestion
signs: Vomiting or diarrhea (may contain blood)
Excessive drooling or foaming at the mouth
Tremors, seizures, or muscle twitching
Dilated or constricted pupils
Pale, blue, or yellow gums
Sudden collapse or loss of coordination
Difficulty breathing
immediate_steps: Remove your pet from the source of the toxin immediately.
Do NOT induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by a veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control.
Collect a sample of the suspected poison (label, container, or plant specimen) to bring to the vet.
Call ASPCA Animal Poison Control: (888) 426-4435 (fee may apply) or your nearest emergency vet.
Keep your pet calm and warm — limit movement to reduce absorption rate.
If toxin is on the skin or fur, rinse the area thoroughly with lukewarm water while wearing gloves.
Note the time of exposure and estimated amount ingested — this is critical information for the vet.
do_not: Do NOT induce vomiting without professional guidance — it can cause additional harm with some toxins (e.g., caustic chemicals, petroleum products).
Do NOT give any home remedies (milk, salt, charcoal) without vet instruction.
Do NOT wait for symptoms to worsen — poisoning is time-sensitive.
Do NOT leave your pet unattended.
when_to_call_vet: Immediately upon suspicion of any toxin ingestion. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.

title: Seizures / Convulsions
signs: Sudden collapse and loss of consciousness
Uncontrolled muscle twitching or jerking
Paddling of the legs (like running while lying down)
Jaw chomping, excessive salivation, or foaming
Loss of bladder or bowel control
Disorientation, staring, or unusual behavior before the seizure (pre-ictal phase)
Confusion, temporary blindness, or restlessness after the seizure (post-ictal phase)
immediate_steps: Stay calm — panicking will not help your pet.
Clear the area of hard or sharp objects to prevent injury during the seizure.
Do NOT restrain your pet — gently guide them away from furniture edges only if safe.
Time the seizure with your phone — seizures lasting over 5 minutes require emergency intervention.
Dim the lights and reduce noise to minimize sensory stimulation.
After the seizure ends, keep your pet in a quiet, darkened room and speak in a calm, soft voice.
Call your vet or emergency animal hospital immediately — even a single first-time seizure warrants evaluation.
Note the duration, type of movements, and any possible triggers.
do_not: Do NOT put your hand or any object in your pet's mouth — they cannot swallow their tongue, and you may be bitten.
Do NOT hold your pet down or restrain their limbs.
Do NOT try to give water or medication during the active seizure.
Do NOT leave your pet alone immediately after a seizure — they may be disoriented and at risk of falling.
when_to_call_vet: Call immediately. Go to an emergency vet if the seizure lasts more than 3–5 minutes, if multiple seizures occur within 24 hours, or if it is your pet's first seizure.

title: Difficulty Breathing
signs: Labored, rapid, or shallow breathing
Open-mouth breathing in cats (always abnormal)
Blue, grey, or white gums or tongue (cyanosis)
Noisy breathing (wheezing, rattling, gurgling)
Extended neck, elbows turned outward (orthopnea posture)
Excessive panting unrelated to exercise or heat
Restlessness and inability to settle
immediate_steps: Keep your pet as calm and still as possible — excitement increases oxygen demand.
Do not force your pet to walk or move unless necessary.
Position your pet in a comfortable, upright posture — do not lay them on their side.
Ensure good air circulation around your pet — open a window if needed.
Transport to an emergency vet immediately — do not delay.
If there is a visible foreign object in the throat, do not attempt blind removal; get professional help.
In the car, keep the temperature cool and windows slightly open.
do_not: Do NOT attempt CPR unless your pet becomes unresponsive and has no heartbeat.
Do NOT muzzle a pet that is having difficulty breathing.
Do NOT offer food or water.
Do NOT leave your pet alone even briefly.
when_to_call_vet: This is a life-threatening emergency. Go to the nearest emergency veterinary clinic immediately — do not call first if your pet is in acute distress.

title: Unresponsive / Collapse
signs: Sudden collapse with inability to rise
Unresponsiveness to touch, voice, or stimulation
Very slow, shallow, or absent breathing
Pale, white, blue, or grey gums
Rapid, weak, or absent pulse
Glazed or fixed eyes
Limp body
immediate_steps: Check for responsiveness — call your pet's name and gently tap a paw.
Check for breathing — watch for chest rise, feel for airflow at the nose/mouth for 10 seconds.
Check for a heartbeat — place your hand on the left chest, just behind the elbow.
If no breathing and no heartbeat, begin pet CPR only if you are trained to do so.
For CPR on dogs: 100–120 chest compressions per minute, 1–2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions.
For CPR on cats: wrap hands around the chest and compress at 100–120 per minute.
Have someone call the emergency vet while you administer CPR.
Transport immediately to an emergency vet — continue CPR in the car if possible with a second person driving.
do_not: Do NOT waste more than 10 seconds assessing — begin CPR quickly if indicated.
Do NOT give water or anything by mouth.
Do NOT leave your pet unattended at any point.
Do NOT administer any medications without veterinary instruction.
when_to_call_vet: Call en route to the emergency clinic. Every second matters — prioritize transport over phone calls.

title: Severe Bleeding
signs: Active, visible bleeding from a wound
Blood soaking through cloth or bandaging rapidly
Coughing or vomiting blood
Blood in urine (red or dark brown urine)
Pale gums, weakness, or rapid collapse (internal bleeding signs)
Distended or rigid abdomen (possible internal hemorrhage)
immediate_steps: Apply direct firm pressure to the wound using a clean cloth, gauze, or towel.
Maintain continuous pressure for at least 5–10 minutes — do not remove the cloth to check the wound.
If blood soaks through, add more material on top without removing the first layer.
Elevate the injured limb above heart level if the wound is on a leg and your pet tolerates it.
Do NOT apply a tourniquet unless the bleeding is life-threatening and uncontrollable — if you must, note the exact time it was applied.
Keep your pet as calm and still as possible — movement increases blood flow.
Transport to an emergency vet immediately while maintaining pressure.
If internal bleeding is suspected (no external wound but pale gums, collapse, distended abdomen), go to the emergency vet without delay.
do_not: Do NOT remove an embedded foreign object (glass, nail, stick) — stabilize it in place.
Do NOT use hydrogen peroxide or alcohol on deep wounds.
Do NOT apply tight bandages that cut off circulation unless trained to do so.
Do NOT delay transport to attempt a full wound cleaning.
when_to_call_vet: Immediately. Any uncontrolled bleeding or suspected internal hemorrhage is a veterinary emergency.

title: Heatstroke / Hyperthermia
signs: Excessive, heavy panting that does not improve with rest
Drooling thick, ropy saliva
Red or dark brick-red gums
High body temperature (above 39.4°C / 103°F)
Vomiting or diarrhea (may contain blood)
Confusion, disorientation, or stumbling
Muscle tremors or seizures
Loss of consciousness
immediate_steps: Move your pet out of the heat immediately — into shade or an air-conditioned space.
Offer small amounts of cool (not ice-cold) water to drink if they are conscious and able to swallow.
Apply cool water to the body, especially the neck, armpits, groin, and paw pads.
Use a fan to increase evaporative cooling — do not cover your pet with wet towels (traps heat).
Do NOT use ice or ice water — rapid cooling can cause dangerous vasoconstriction.
Take your pet's temperature rectally if possible — target cooling to below 39.4°C / 103°F.
Transport to an emergency vet immediately — even if your pet appears to recover, internal damage can be severe.
Continue cooling during transport with the car's air conditioning on full.
do_not: Do NOT use ice, ice packs, or ice water — this causes shock and slows cooling.
Do NOT cover your pet with wet towels.
Do NOT force water into an unconscious pet.
Do NOT assume your pet is 'fine' if they cool down — organ damage may have occurred.
when_to_call_vet: Immediately. Heatstroke causes irreversible organ damage within minutes. Even if your pet seems to recover, a vet assessment is mandatory.

title: Choking / Airway Obstruction
signs: Pawing or clawing at the mouth or throat
Gagging, retching, or repeated swallowing
High-pitched wheezing or whistling sound when breathing
Blue or purple gums or tongue (severe oxygen deprivation)
Extreme distress, panic, or sudden inability to vocalize
Collapse in severe cases
immediate_steps: Stay calm and approach your pet carefully — a choking, panicked animal may bite.
Open your pet's mouth carefully and look inside — only remove a visible object if you can safely grasp it with two fingers.
Do NOT do a blind finger sweep — you may push the object deeper.
For a small dog or cat: hold them face-down with your hands around their waist and give 3–5 firm thrusts between the shoulder blades.
For a large dog: place your hands below the rib cage, make a fist, and give 3–5 firm upward and forward thrusts (modified Heimlich).
Check the mouth again for the dislodged object after each set of thrusts.
If unsuccessful after 2 rounds, rush to the nearest emergency vet without delay.
If your pet loses consciousness, begin rescue breathing (1 breath every 3 seconds into the nose, with mouth held closed).
do_not: Do NOT attempt blind sweeps of the throat with your fingers.
Do NOT use excessive force that could injure ribs — use firm but controlled pressure.
Do NOT waste time on multiple attempts if the airway is clearly fully blocked — go to the vet.
Do NOT let the pet eat or drink even if the object is removed until cleared by a vet.
when_to_call_vet: Immediately — call en route. Even if you successfully dislodge the object, internal injury may have occurred and a vet check is required.

title: Suspected Fracture / Broken Bone
signs: Sudden non-weight-bearing lameness after trauma
Visible deformity, swelling, or abnormal limb angle
Grinding or crepitus (crackling sound) on movement
Bone visible through the skin (open/compound fracture)
Extreme pain — crying, snapping, or withdrawal when touched
Inability to move the affected limb
Dragging of hindlimbs (possible spinal involvement)
immediate_steps: Minimize movement — keep your pet as still as possible.
Gently muzzle your pet if there is a bite risk — even gentle pets may bite when in severe pain.
Do NOT attempt to set or straighten the bone.
For an open (compound) fracture: cover the exposed bone loosely with a clean, damp cloth — do not apply pressure.
Support the injured limb by sliding a rigid surface (board, magazine) underneath without lifting the limb.
For spinal injuries (hind limb paralysis): slide your pet onto a rigid flat surface (board or tray) and transport without bending the spine.
Keep your pet warm — shock is a real risk with severe trauma.
Transport to an emergency vet immediately using a makeshift stretcher.
do_not: Do NOT try to set, splint, or bandage the fracture yourself without training.
Do NOT give human pain medications (ibuprofen, acetaminophen, aspirin) — these are toxic to pets.
Do NOT allow your pet to walk on the injured limb.
Do NOT delay transport — fractures worsen rapidly with movement and untreated shock.
when_to_call_vet: Immediately. All suspected fractures and spinal injuries require emergency veterinary radiographs and treatment.
